After each action, compare achieved motion with intended motion and update clearance and contact predictions when tracking differs. Recover the intended attitude in verified clearance or choose a more controllable configuration rather than accumulating deviations. When holding an object, preserve verified retention during correction or re-support it before reconfiguring.
lessons.why: The policy repeatedly copied measured orientation into the next target despite claiming to preserve its established attitude. This converted tracking deviations into accepted goals during both approach and lift. The original rule was sound but insufficiently operationalized; explicitly separating persistent goals from feedback would prevent this drift.

lessons.lesson: Before sensing, identify the uncertainty that will change the next action and select visible surfaces that resolve it. Reuse established geometry while observations remain consistent; refresh it after contact changes, object motion, or tracking error makes it uncertain. Prefer targeted checks of unresolved clearance, contact alignment, attitude, or retention over repeated broad localization. If the target is obscured, retain its last confirmed geometry as a provisional collision constraint and inspect another view or make a clearance-checked adjustment that exposes useful features. If visibility loss recurs, change the approach rather than repeating the same maneuver.
lessons.why: Numerous depth batches and previews repeatedly established the same target and support geometry, contributing substantial sensing overhead. Those measurements were useful initially, but later effort should have shifted toward object attitude and hand-relative motion rather than further localization and height-only confirmation.

reflections.diagnosis: The policy successfully captured and lifted the mug, but failed the upright-grasp requirement. The evaluator confirms a 0.2381 m lift and retention for two seconds, while reporting upright_grasp=false and a pre-closure tilt of 19.29 degrees. During the open-hand approach, contact tipped the mug at steps 3–4; the policy continued to describe it as upright and closed without correcting the disturbed pose. Subsequent orientation tracking errors accumulated because commands repeatedly adopted the latest measured quaternion as the new attitude goal. Tilt reached about 42 degrees. Depth sensing was useful for initial localization and support clearance, but extensive probing did not consistently produce a coherent object-attitude estimate or trigger recovery. Repeated retention lifts and holds postponed deliberate correction until step 28, increased cropping, and consumed substantial calls. That correction improved attitude temporarily but had a large tracking error; subsequent holds again adopted the drifting measured attitude. Physical retention was achieved, but upright acquisition and sustained attitude control were not.
reflections.failure_mode: Non-upright grasp following unaddressed approach contact, compounded by measured-pose goal drift and an open-ended retention-verification loop.

lessons_review.lesson: Before approaching or changing contact, use observed target geometry and the measured hand configuration to check the complete swept hand, arm, and any held object against the target, support, and surroundings. Support clearance and endpoint clearance do not establish a clear approach. Establish the intended attitude in verified clearance, then align opposing solid contact regions arranged to resist unwanted rotation. Close in place once alignment and the closing sweep are verified. If an unsecured object moves unexpectedly, unload along a clear path, observe its settled pose, and revise the contact alignment or approach before continuing.
lessons_review.why: Clearance checks rejected low approaches, closure occurred in place, and no hand-table or self-collisions were recorded. However, execution emphasized minimum hand height rather than target intersection: approach contact tilted the mug at steps 3–4, and the prescribed recovery was not applied before step 5. Preserve this rule while making task-compatible object attitude an explicit pre-closure condition.

lessons_review.lesson: After acquiring or changing a grasp, perform a cautious retention test. During motion and holding, verify object displacement, task-required attitude, and hand-relative stability separately, using corresponding visible features and targeted depth on identifiable, spatially separated surfaces. A stationary palm or closed gripper does not establish object stability. If the object rotates or slips, make a bounded attitude correction only when reliable hand-object motion is verified; otherwise re-support it and change the grasp. Count a required hold only while all task conditions remain verified, and finish once those conditions and the executed duration satisfy the task.
lessons_review.why: The initial retention lift at step 6 was useful, but the verification prerequisite became a recurring reason to postpone correction. Steps 12–19 and 21–27 repeatedly tested retention despite acknowledged tilt, instead of selecting correction or re-support. The recovery clause was not followed. Rewrite the rule so each test must produce an actionable decision, rather than another equivalent test.

lessons_review.lesson: Keep explicit task-compatible position and attitude goals separate from measured pose. Use the measured state to construct bounded commands toward those goals, not to silently replace them. After each action, compare achieved motion with intended motion and update clearance and contact predictions when tracking differs. Recover the intended attitude in verified clearance or choose a more controllable configuration rather than accumulating deviations. When holding an object, preserve verified retention during correction or re-support it before reconfiguring.
lessons_review.why: This principle directly addressed the observed problem but was not implemented. Commands through much of steps 6–27 copied the latest measured quaternion while claiming unchanged attitude. At step 28, the requested correction had a 0.4638 rad orientation tracking gap; steps 29–30 again adopted the resulting measured poses. Retain and sharpen the distinction between feedback and the persistent goal.

lessons_review.lesson: Before sensing, identify the uncertainty that will change the next action and select visible surfaces that resolve it. Reuse established geometry while observations remain consistent; refresh it after contact changes, object motion, or tracking error makes it uncertain. Prefer targeted checks of unresolved clearance, contact alignment, attitude, or retention over repeated broad localization. If the target is obscured, retain its last confirmed geometry as a provisional collision constraint and inspect another view or make a clearance-checked adjustment that exposes useful features. If visibility loss recurs, change the approach rather than repeating the same maneuver.
lessons_review.why: Initial depth queries established useful target and support geometry, and step 20 improved visibility. Nevertheless, broad probe batches continued without resolving attitude, while further lifts repeatedly cropped the target. Some queried points landed on the support or robot rather than the intended surface. The rule needs a more explicit requirement for surface identity, geometric consistency, and a decision after sensing.

lessons.lesson: Treat the task-required object attitude as a constraint during approach and contact acquisition, not merely after lifting. Check the complete swept hand, arm, and any held object against observed geometry; support clearance alone does not establish a clear approach. Establish hand attitude in free space and align opposing solid contact regions that resist unwanted rotation. If an unsecured target shifts or rotates unexpectedly, unload along a clear path, observe its settled pose, and restore a task-compatible pose or revise the approach. Close in place only after the target pose, contact alignment, and closing sweep are verified.
lessons.why: Support-clearance checks prevented table collisions but missed target contact during the open-hand approach. Tilt increased before closure, and the evaluator specifically rejected the resulting non-upright grasp. Responding to the disturbed pose before closing addresses the primary failure.

lessons.lesson: Maintain explicit task-compatible position and attitude goals separately from measured pose. Use measurements to construct bounded commands toward those goals; do not redefine a hold goal by copying each newly measured pose. After acting, compare achieved hand motion and object attitude with the intended change. If tracking deviates, revise the motion prediction and make a clearance-checked correction while retention remains reliable. If corrections are poorly tracked or the object moves unpredictably relative to the hand, re-support the object and choose a more controllable arm configuration or grasp before resuming.
lessons.why: Repeatedly adopting measured orientation accumulated substantial tilt despite claims of unchanged attitude. The late correction demonstrated that commanded and achieved rotation could differ greatly. Persistent goals and explicit response to tracking error are needed both during lifting and holding.

lessons.lesson: Make each cautious retention test lead to a decision. If corresponding object features follow the hand reliably and task conditions are satisfied, proceed to the next required action or execute the remaining hold. If retention is reliable but attitude is wrong, correct attitude in verified clearance instead of adding more displacement or repeating the same hold. If retention remains ambiguous, obtain a more informative view or measurement; if uncertainty persists, re-support and revise the grasp. Count holding time only while all required conditions remain verified, and finish when the task is satisfied.
lessons.why: The policy repeatedly promised correction after another retention test, despite substantial elevation and continuous capture. Additional lifts worsened visibility, and repeated stationary holds did not resolve the known attitude defect. A mandatory decision after testing would reduce both failure risk and the significant sensing/action waste.

lessons.lesson: Choose depth queries to resolve the uncertainty that changes the next action. Identify which visible target surface each sample belongs to, reject hand or background returns and inconsistent samples, and estimate spatial attitude from a coherent surface or identifiable object axis. Do not infer attitude from an upright-looking projection or similar heights of unrelated points. Track corresponding features to assess displacement, attitude, and hand-relative stability separately. Reuse geometry while observations remain consistent; if useful features are obscured or estimates disagree, inspect another view or make a clearance-checked visibility adjustment before selecting the next manipulation action.
lessons.why: Depth provided enough information to notice target motion and later substantial tilt, but the policy alternated between recognizing tilt and describing the target as upright or nearly level. Numerous changing sample locations, occasional background returns, and cropping made informal height comparisons unreliable. Coherent feature-based estimation would make sensing actionable rather than repetitive.

reflections.diagnosis: The episode failed before grasp acquisition. The only action changed palm orientation while keeping its target position fixed; execution aborted on contact between the right shoulder yaw link and the torso. The hand never contacted the mug, the gripper never closed, and no lift occurred. Depth sensing usefully established target surfaces and tabletop height, but those measurements did not validate the whole-arm motion. The preview checked the hand's lowest point, and endpoint IK was accurate, yet neither established self-collision clearance during the orientation change. The decisive missing check concerned the arm relative to the robot's body, not the mug's location.
reflections.failure_mode: Whole-arm self-collision during a fixed-position palm reorientation, before any grasp attempt.

lessons_review.lesson: Treat the task-required object attitude as a constraint during approach and contact acquisition, not merely after lifting. Check the complete swept hand, arm, and any held object against observed geometry; support clearance alone does not establish a clear approach. Establish hand attitude in free space and align opposing solid contact regions that resist unwanted rotation. If an unsecured target shifts or rotates unexpectedly, unload along a clear path, observe its settled pose, and restore a task-compatible pose or revise the approach. Close in place only after the target pose, contact alignment, and closing sweep are verified.
lessons_review.why: At step 1, the policy explicitly followed the instruction to establish attitude in free space, but did not adequately apply the whole-arm clearance requirement. The preview reported hand height rather than arm–body clearance. The principle remains valid, but needs an explicit distinction between free space around the hand and a safe arm configuration, plus an alternative to fixed-position rotation.

lessons_review.lesson: Maintain explicit task-compatible position and attitude goals separately from measured pose. Use measurements to construct bounded commands toward those goals; do not redefine a hold goal by copying each newly measured pose. After acting, compare achieved hand motion and object attitude with the intended change. If tracking deviates, revise the motion prediction and make a clearance-checked correction while retention remains reliable. If corrections are poorly tracked or the object moves unpredictably relative to the hand, re-support the object and choose a more controllable arm configuration or grasp before resuming.
lessons_review.why: The episode ended during the initial orientation change at step 1. There was no retained object, hold-goal drift, or opportunity to evaluate corrective tracking. Preserve these safeguards without attributing the abort to a retention or tracking failure.

lessons_review.lesson: Make each cautious retention test lead to a decision. If corresponding object features follow the hand reliably and task conditions are satisfied, proceed to the next required action or execute the remaining hold. If retention is reliable but attitude is wrong, correct attitude in verified clearance instead of adding more displacement or repeating the same hold. If retention remains ambiguous, obtain a more informative view or measurement; if uncertainty persists, re-support and revise the grasp. Count holding time only while all required conditions remain verified, and finish when the task is satisfied.
lessons_review.why: No retention test or hold occurred before the step 1 abort. This rule was untested and did not contribute to the failure.

lessons_review.lesson: Choose depth queries to resolve the uncertainty that changes the next action. Identify which visible target surface each sample belongs to, reject hand or background returns and inconsistent samples, and estimate spatial attitude from a coherent surface or identifiable object axis. Do not infer attitude from an upright-looking projection or similar heights of unrelated points. Track corresponding features to assess displacement, attitude, and hand-relative stability separately. Reuse geometry while observations remain consistent; if useful features are obscured or estimates disagree, inspect another view or make a clearance-checked visibility adjustment before selecting the next manipulation action.
lessons_review.why: At step 1, depth samples provided useful metric information about the mug and support surface, rather than relying solely on image appearance. However, this geometric information addressed target and table clearance, not the arm–body clearance that determined whether the chosen action could execute.

lessons.lesson: Treat a palm orientation change as a whole-arm motion, even when the palm position stays fixed. Use available camera views and measured joints to assess arm–body clearance as well as clearance from surrounding geometry, including any held object. Hand clearance and endpoint reachability are not substitutes for checking the arm's sweep. If an in-place rotation crowds the arm against the body or its clearance is uncertain, inspect the other available views and choose a better-separated waypoint; move toward it while largely preserving attitude, then blend the needed rotation into the approach. Use bounded increments and recheck visible arm clearance and measured tracking before continuing.
lessons.why: The fixed-position orientation command caused shoulder–torso contact despite ample hand–table clearance and accurate endpoint IK. A configuration-aware approach, rather than assuming the hand's free space applied to the whole arm, directly addresses the failure.

lessons.lesson: Maintain explicit task-compatible position and attitude goals rather than replacing them with each newly measured pose. Plan approach and contact acquisition to preserve the required target attitude, align opposing contact regions that resist unwanted motion, and clear the closing sweep. If an unsecured target shifts unexpectedly, unload along an observed clear path, observe its settled pose, and restore a compatible pose or revise the approach before closing. After acting, compare achieved hand motion and target attitude with the intended change. Correct in verified clearance while retention is reliable; otherwise re-support the target and choose a more controllable arm configuration or grasp.
lessons.why: The initial action pursued a task-compatible grasp attitude, but the abort prevented contact acquisition or tracking evaluation. This retains the useful attitude, contact, and goal-tracking safeguards while allowing configuration changes instead of requiring orientation to be completed at a fixed palm location.

lessons.lesson: Make each cautious retention test lead to a decision. If corresponding object features follow the hand reliably and task conditions are satisfied, proceed to the next required action or execute the remaining hold. If retention is reliable but attitude is wrong, correct attitude in verified clearance instead of adding displacement or repeating the same hold. If retention remains ambiguous, obtain a more informative view or measurement; if uncertainty persists, re-support the object and revise the grasp. Count holding time only while all required conditions remain verified, and finish when the task is satisfied.
lessons.why: Retained as an untested safeguard: the episode terminated before any grasp or lift, so there is no evidence that this decision-oriented retention rule needs removal.

lessons.lesson: Choose depth queries to resolve uncertainty that changes the next action. Associate each sample with a visible target surface, reject hand or background returns and inconsistent samples, and estimate attitude from a coherent surface or identifiable object axis. Do not infer spatial attitude from an upright-looking projection or similar heights of unrelated points. Track corresponding features to assess displacement, attitude, and hand-relative stability separately. Reuse geometry while observations remain consistent. When the unresolved issue is arm clearance rather than target geometry, inspect the relevant arm and body views and revise the approach instead of collecting more target samples.
lessons.why: The depth samples supported useful target localization, but additional target geometry would not establish shoulder–torso clearance. The revision preserves good depth practice while directing sensing toward the uncertainty that actually constrains the next motion.

reflections.diagnosis: The episode failed during approach, before a grasp was established. Depth sensing usefully distinguished the tabletop from the mug rim, but the policy primarily used those estimates and pose previews to check hand–table clearance. It did not establish clearance between the complete open hand and the mug along the approach, or align the mug within opposing grasp contacts. Simulator truth shows middle-finger contact during the first move and continued contact during the second, when the mug tilted about 19 degrees. Neither move caused a reported table or self-collision, but those checks did not establish a safe target-relative approach. The final palm attitude also differed substantially from the requested attitude, making the intended hand geometry unreliable. Both commands kept the gripper open; the recorded episode ended without closure, verified retention, or a hold. The approximately 1.3 cm rise occurred while the mug still touched the table and did not satisfy the requested upright lift. Four depth batches totaling 27 samples produced useful scene estimates, but did not resolve the clearance uncertainty that actually determined success.
reflections.failure_mode: Unilateral contact during an open-hand approach disturbed the target before opposing grasp contacts were established. Table clearance and palm reachability were treated as insufficient substitutes for target-relative swept-hand clearance and verified attitude tracking.

lessons_review.lesson: Treat a palm orientation change as a whole-arm motion, even when the palm position stays fixed.
lessons_review.why: The policy explicitly preserved attitude during the first translation and blended a modest requested rotation into the second approach. No self-collision or hand–table contact was reported. This addressed arm and environmental clearance, but did not prevent contact with the target itself; the revised rule retains whole-arm checking while emphasizing measured pose tracking.

lessons_review.lesson: Maintain explicit task-compatible position and attitude goals rather than replacing them with each newly measured pose.
lessons_review.why: The policy maintained an approach goal, but did not operationalize the lesson's opposing-contact and closing-sweep requirements before advancing. The target tilted during the second action while the gripper remained open. There was no subsequent action in which the prescribed unloading or restoration behavior could be assessed.

lessons_review.lesson: Make each cautious retention test lead to a decision.
lessons_review.why: No closure, retention test, or holding action occurred. The rule neither caused stalling nor demonstrated a benefit here. Its decision-making structure remains useful after contact acquisition and is retained in the revised set.

lessons_review.lesson: Choose depth queries to resolve uncertainty that changes the next action.
lessons_review.why: The samples supported useful table and rim estimates, but the policy collected additional batches without demonstrating a target-relative swept-hand clearance check. The revised rule explicitly connects depth estimates to measured hand geometry and redirects sensing toward the unresolved approach hazard.

lessons.lesson: Plan contact using the complete hand configuration and its swept path, not just the palm position or clearance above a support surface. Use the available views and measured hand configuration to align the target between opposing contact regions while keeping the approach and closing sweep clear. If part of the hand would strike the target before that alignment is achieved, choose a clear offset approach and establish the needed attitude before advancing. If an unsecured target moves unexpectedly, unload along an observed clear path, reobserve its pose, and restore compatible support or revise the approach before closing.
lessons.why: The previews emphasized the lowest hand point relative to the table, yet target contact occurred during both open-hand moves. The second move tilted the mug before a grasp existed. A full hand-to-target sweep check would address the actual collision mechanism.

lessons.lesson: Maintain explicit task-compatible pose goals and compare achieved palm motion, attitude, and joint configuration with the intended change after each action. Treat reorientation as a whole-arm sweep, including any held object, and inspect body and surrounding clearance. If attitude tracking degrades or clearance becomes uncertain, inspect a more informative available view and choose a verified-clear waypoint or better arm configuration before resuming the approach. Preserve attitude while leaving constrained geometry, then blend reorientation into verified clearance; if retention is unreliable, re-support the object before reconfiguring.
lessons.why: The first move largely tracked its goal, but the second ended with approximately 0.945 radians of attitude error despite close position tracking and a reachable IK request. This makes measured attitude and configuration essential to any subsequent approach or recovery. Whole-arm caution remains worth preserving because no self-collision was reported.

lessons.lesson: Choose depth samples to resolve the geometric uncertainty that changes the next action. Associate returns with identifiable target surfaces or relevant obstacles, reject unintended hand or background returns, and compare the resulting geometry with the measured hand configuration to select a clear approach and opposing contacts. Infer attitude from coherent surfaces or corresponding features rather than unrelated samples. Reuse geometry while observations remain consistent. If surface identity is ambiguous, inspect another available view before adding samples; if the unresolved issue is arm clearance or pose tracking, inspect the relevant images and proprioception instead of resampling the target.
lessons.why: The policy obtained table and rim estimates from 27 samples, but those estimates did not prevent open-finger contact. The useful next sensing objective was target-relative hand clearance, not another broad collection of surface heights.

lessons.lesson: Once the target is aligned within opposing contact regions and the closing sweep is clear, close and perform a cautious, task-compatible retention test. Track corresponding object features to verify hand-relative stability separately from required displacement and attitude. If retention and task conditions are verified, proceed to the next required action or complete the remaining hold. If retention is reliable but attitude is wrong, correct it in verified clearance. If retention is ambiguous, obtain a more informative view or measurement; if it remains unreliable, re-support the object and revise the grasp. Count holding time only while the required conditions remain verified.
lessons.why: The episode ended with an open gripper, a tilted mug still touching the table, and no verified hold. A concrete acquisition-to-verification sequence distinguishes incidental contact-induced motion from a successful grasp and lift without encouraging repeated inconclusive tests.

reflections.diagnosis: The episode failed before acquiring a grasp. Depth sensing usefully established the target and support geometry, and measured hand geometry informed caution about low-finger clearance. However, the policy emphasized clearance above the table rather than clearance between the target and the full moving hand. Simulator truth shows unilateral middle-finger contact during every action. The leveling action at step 3 produced an achieved orientation error of about 0.375 rad and target tilt up to 6.6 degrees; further advance and reorientation at step 4 increased tilt to 27.3 degrees. The policy did not establish a verified-clear recovery path or opposing-contact alignment. All four commands kept the gripper open. The evaluator recorded only 1.87 cm of lift, no upright grasp, and no sustained hold. Sensor use was therefore partially useful but poorly connected to action selection: 50 depth samples and eight pose previews did not resolve the decisive uncertainties about target-side clearance, rotation tracking, and grasp alignment. Reobservation after target movement was warranted, but repeated broad localization was not a substitute for those checks.
reflections.failure_mode: Unilateral open-hand contact during approach and poorly tracked reorientation displaced and tilted the target before grasp acquisition. No closure, verified lift, or hold followed.

lessons_review.lesson: Plan contact using the complete hand configuration and its swept path, not just the palm position or clearance above a support surface.
lessons_review.why: Partially helped: steps 1–3 used measured fingertip geometry and previews to avoid low-hand approaches, and no hand-table contact was recorded. However, the policy applied the lesson mainly to vertical support clearance, not to the hand's lateral and rotational sweep against the target. Contact occurred in every action. Retain the principle but make target-side clearance and opposing-contact alignment explicit.

lessons_review.lesson: Maintain explicit task-compatible pose goals and compare achieved palm motion, attitude, and joint configuration with the intended change after each action.
lessons_review.why: The policy inspected measured configurations, but successive approach commands adopted the newly measured attitude rather than clearly maintaining an independent grasp-attitude goal. At step 3, rotation tracking degraded substantially; step 4 nevertheless resumed approach and reorientation near the target. This is incomplete application of the rule, not evidence that clearance-aware reconfiguration was harmful.

lessons_review.lesson: Choose depth samples to resolve the geometric uncertainty that changes the next action.
lessons_review.why: Initial samples localized the target surfaces and table without privileged object coordinates. Later sampling repeatedly revisited rim, body, and support geometry without demonstrating a resolved closing corridor or handling the orientation mismatch. The instruction to reuse consistent geometry remains valuable; strengthen the requirement to connect each query to a specific motion decision.

lessons_review.lesson: Once the target is aligned within opposing contact regions and the closing sweep is clear, close and perform a cautious, task-compatible retention test.
lessons_review.why: No closure or retention test occurred, and the available evidence does not establish that the observed poses were safe to close from. Keep the conditional transition to closure and verification. The remedy is to achieve real opposing-contact alignment and then test retention, not simply to close earlier.

lessons.lesson: Check the full measured hand shape and its approach and closing sweeps against the observed target and surroundings, not just the palm position or clearance above a support. Use an informative view to place the intended grasp region between opposing contact regions without a projecting digit entering the target first. If the path is obstructed, use an observed clear offset, establish the grasp attitude there, and then approach. If an unsecured target shifts during an open-hand motion, unload the apparent contact along a clear path, reobserve its pose and support, and revise the approach before continuing.
lessons.why: All actions maintained table clearance but produced unilateral target contact. The policy's reasoning repeatedly emphasized the lowest finger and support height, while target tilt increased during reorientation and further approach. Explicitly checking the target-side sweep would address the actual collision mechanism.

lessons.lesson: Keep the intended task-compatible attitude separate from the measured attitude; do not adopt tracking drift as the next desired attitude. After each action, compare achieved translation, rotation, and joint configuration with the intended change before advancing. If rotation behaves unexpectedly, inspect the available views for clearance of the hand, arm, and any held object. Preserve attitude while leaving constrained geometry along a verified-clear path, then correct it in clearance and recheck alignment before returning. Re-support an unreliably retained object before reconfiguring.
lessons.why: Steps 1 and 2 carried forward measured attitudes as the fingers progressively lowered relative to the palm. Step 3's attempted leveling had a large orientation-tracking error and disturbed the target. Step 4 continued near-target motion rather than establishing a clear configuration for correction.

lessons.lesson: When current images and measured hand configuration establish opposing-contact alignment and a clear closing sweep, close and perform a cautious, task-compatible retention test rather than continuing open-hand adjustments. Track corresponding target features to verify stability relative to the hand, and independently verify required displacement and attitude relative to the surroundings. If verified, proceed with the task and count any required holding time only while those conditions remain satisfied. If verification is ambiguous, obtain a more informative view; if retention is unreliable, re-support the object and revise the grasp. Correct retained-object attitude only in verified clearance.
lessons.why: The recorded episode consisted entirely of open-hand adjustments. Target movement never became a verified grasp or sustained lift. This preserves the necessary safety condition while providing a concrete progression from alignment to closure, retention testing, and task completion.

lessons.lesson: Choose each depth query to resolve an uncertainty that changes the next action, such as a contact-bearing surface or a limiting obstacle along the hand sweep. Associate samples with recognizable surfaces and distinguish intended contact surfaces from hand, support, interior, or background returns. Infer attitude from corresponding features or coherent surfaces. Reuse established geometry while observations remain consistent. When occlusion, arm clearance, or pose tracking is the bottleneck, inspect a more informative available view and measured configuration, then select a revised motion instead of repeating broad target sampling.
lessons.why: The policy obtained 50 depth samples across four actions, yet its decisions remained focused on rim/support height rather than the relevant contact corridor. Some remeasurement was justified by target disturbance, but resolving view ambiguity and actual hand motion would have been more useful than repeatedly surveying the same broad geometry.

reflections.diagnosis: The mug was successfully grasped, lifted 12.97 cm, and retained for the required duration, but the evaluator rejected the episode because upright_grasp was false; it recorded a pre-close tilt of 7.7 degrees. The approach disturbed the unsecured mug, and the policy did not reliably distinguish the mug's attitude from the palm's attitude. Open-hand motions produced tipping at steps 15 and 31, and the subsequent lift included a transient tilt of 27.3 degrees at step 35. Depth was useful for locating the mug, distinguishing it from the table, and confirming elevation. However, repeated broad sampling did not resolve the actual bottlenecks: unstable rotational tracking, contact alignment, and object attitude. Descriptions such as 'opening facing upward' or 'level palm' were treated as stronger evidence of uprightness than they warranted. The episode also incurred substantial avoidable cost: repeated orientation corrections and retreats, followed by sixteen holding actions at steps 37–52 despite an already retained, elevated grasp.
reflections.failure_mode: Upright-grasp verification failure despite successful lifting and retention, compounded by oscillatory orientation correction, redundant depth sampling, and failure to exit the holding phase.

lessons_review.lesson: Check the full measured hand shape and its approach and closing sweeps against the observed target and surroundings, not just the palm position or clearance above a support.
lessons_review.why: Whole-hand clearance checks and offset approaches avoided executed hand-table collisions. Withdrawal at step 16 also removed contact after the disturbance at step 15. However, clearance above the table repeatedly substituted for clearance from the mug, and the open-hand tipping at step 31 was not followed by explicit verification and restoration of the target's task-compatible attitude. Keep the sweep-checking principle and strengthen the target-state check before closure.

lessons_review.lesson: Keep the intended task-compatible attitude separate from the measured attitude; do not adopt tracking drift as the next desired attitude.
lessons_review.why: The distinction was useful, and moving outward after the rejected shoulder-torso collision at step 5 enabled step 6. But establishing an exact level attitude became a repeated prerequisite rather than a bounded correction process. Steps 1–12 and 17–23 repeatedly corrected, raised, or withdrew the hand while rotation oscillated, even when translation tracked well. Shorter actions eventually helped, but the rule lacked an explicit transition from adequate alignment to task progress or to a different reachable approach. During the final holds, measured position was also repeatedly adopted as the next target, allowing accumulated positional drift.

lessons_review.lesson: When current images and measured hand configuration establish opposing-contact alignment and a clear closing sweep, close and perform a cautious, task-compatible retention test rather than continuing open-hand adjustments.
lessons_review.why: Closure at step 33 and the cautious lift at step 34 established a retained grasp; subsequent actions achieved the required elevation and duration. The independent object-attitude check was not implemented convincingly, however, and steps 37–52 repeatedly extended the hold instead of completing the task. Preserve the close-and-test sequence, but make object-based attitude verification, recovery, elapsed-time accounting, and completion explicit.

lessons_review.lesson: Choose each depth query to resolve an uncertainty that changes the next action, associate samples with recognizable surfaces, and reuse established geometry while observations remain consistent.
lessons_review.why: Initial depth samples established useful target and support geometry, and the wrist view became informative when the head view cropped the grasp at steps 30–34. Nevertheless, nearly every action was preceded by renewed sampling, including long periods when rotational tracking rather than target location was the bottleneck. Some purported target samples returned the hand, table, or interior. Later attitude claims relied on selected similar-height returns rather than a coherent, spatially distributed set of corresponding features. The principle should remain, with a clearer requirement to connect each query to a pending decision.

lessons.lesson: Before making or changing contact, verify the target's task-required attitude relative to its support or stable surroundings independently of palm attitude. Use an informative view and the measured hand shape to align opposing contact regions and check the entire approach and closing sweep against both the target and its surroundings. If an unsecured target moves or tips during open-hand motion, unload the apparent contact along an observed clear path, reobserve its pose and support, and restore a task-compatible supported pose or choose a revised grasp before continuing.
lessons.why: The hand remained clear of the table but still disturbed the mug during approach. Step 31 produced a tipping event before the eventual closure, and the evaluator specifically rejected upright_grasp while accepting lift and retention. Checking the target's pose and the complete target-relative sweep would address the missing condition rather than merely adding more support-clearance checks.

lessons.lesson: Maintain an explicit task-compatible pose goal for each motion, distinct from the measured pose. If achieved rotations overshoot or alternate, inspect arm and hand clearance and try shorter, smaller corrections in clear space. If tracking remains unreliable, change to a clearance-checked reachable configuration or approach instead of repeating the same correction or retreat. Once the achieved configuration provides the required alignment and safe sweep, advance the task rather than seeking exact nominal attitude. Re-support an unreliably retained object before reconfiguring.
lessons.why: Early rotational errors were large despite accurate palm translation, and repeated attempts to establish a level attitude consumed many actions without approaching the mug. Shortened commands at steps 11–12 demonstrated a useful adaptation. Later correction and retreat loops show why the rule also needs a geometry-based acceptance condition and an alternative approach when tracking does not improve.

lessons.lesson: Once opposing-contact alignment and a clear closing sweep are established, close and perform a cautious retention test without unnecessary simultaneous reorientation. Track corresponding target features relative to the hand to detect slip and relative to stable surroundings to verify the required displacement and attitude; a level palm or upward-facing surface alone is insufficient. Correct a reliably retained target's attitude only in verified clearance; otherwise re-support it and revise the grasp. During a hold, preserve the intended pose rather than replacing it with measured drift, accumulate executed time only while the required conditions remain verified, and finish or advance to the next task stage when those conditions are complete.
lessons.why: The close-and-test sequence achieved retention, but object attitude was not established by the level palm command. The lift exhibited a substantial transient tilt, and later holds showed increasing tilt despite nearly level measured palm orientation. Sixteen holding actions added cost and further drift after the evaluator's retention requirement was satisfied. Explicit object-based verification and a completion transition would improve both reliability and efficiency.

lessons.lesson: Before querying depth, identify the uncertainty and how each possible result would change the next action. Sample recognizable target or obstacle surfaces, rejecting hand, support, interior, and background returns that do not represent the intended feature. Estimate attitude from corresponding features distributed across the target or from a coherent surface, not from isolated similar-height samples. Reuse established geometry while observations remain consistent. When occlusion or pose tracking is the bottleneck, inspect the most informative available view and measured configuration, then revise the motion; obtain further depth only for the specific unresolved geometric decision.
lessons.why: Depth successfully localized the mug and support and later confirmed elevation, but repeated broad batches continued through orientation-only adjustments and stable holding. Several batches mixed target returns with hand, support, or interior returns. More deliberate surface association and distributed attitude evidence would have been more informative than repeated broad sampling, while reducing the episode's substantial sensing and reasoning cost.

reflections.diagnosis: The episode failed before establishing a grasp. Depth use was useful for initial target localization and support-height estimation, but those estimates were not converted into a safe whole-hand approach. The policy emphasized fingertip clearance above the table without adequately checking the fingers' swept volume against the mug. During step 2, substantial orientation tracking error accompanied open-hand contact and tipping. At step 3, the policy still described the mug as upright and attempted an in-place wrist correction while the hand overlapped it; tipping increased to about 51.5 degrees. Similar-height depth samples did not establish a coherent object attitude, and the measured orientation error should have changed the motion strategy. No closing command occurred. The evaluator's 3.2 cm displacement was not a retained upright lift, and no qualifying hold was achieved. Repeated depth sampling added cost without resolving the main bottleneck: contact-aware motion under unreliable orientation tracking.
reflections.failure_mode: Unsecured-target tipping caused by an open-hand approach followed by an in-place orientation correction near contact; no opposing-contact grasp, verified lift, or hold.

lessons_review.lesson: Before making or changing contact, verify the target's task-required attitude relative to its support or stable surroundings independently of palm attitude. Use an informative view and the measured hand shape to align opposing contact regions and check the entire approach and closing sweep against both the target and its surroundings. If an unsecured target moves or tips during open-hand motion, unload the apparent contact along an observed clear path, reobserve its pose and support, and restore a task-compatible supported pose or choose a revised grasp before continuing.
lessons_review.why: Support clearance was considered, but the essential target-clearance and unloading requirements were not enforced. Step 2 introduced open-hand contact and tipping; step 3 changed orientation instead of separating and reassessing. The principle remains sound, but should make explicit that table clearance does not establish target clearance.

lessons_review.lesson: Maintain an explicit task-compatible pose goal for each motion, distinct from the measured pose. If achieved rotations overshoot or alternate, inspect arm and hand clearance and try shorter, smaller corrections in clear space. If tracking remains unreliable, change to a clearance-checked reachable configuration or approach instead of repeating the same correction or retreat. Once the achieved configuration provides the required alignment and safe sweep, advance the task rather than seeking exact nominal attitude. Re-support an unreliably retained object before reconfiguring.
lessons_review.why: Step 3 used a shorter correction, but not in clear space. The preceding orientation gap was about 0.46 rad, yet the next action rotated beside the unsecured target. The lesson did not cause the failure; its clearance prerequisite was bypassed. The revision should tie measured tracking discrepancies directly to replanning the digit sweep.

lessons_review.lesson: Once opposing-contact alignment and a clear closing sweep are established, close and perform a cautious retention test without unnecessary simultaneous reorientation. Track corresponding target features relative to the hand to detect slip and relative to stable surroundings to verify the required displacement and attitude; a level palm or upward-facing surface alone is insufficient. Correct a reliably retained target's attitude only in verified clearance; otherwise re-support it and revise the grasp. During a hold, preserve the intended pose rather than replacing it with measured drift, accumulate executed time only while the required conditions remain verified, and finish or advance to the next task stage when those conditions are complete.
lessons_review.why: The episode never reached closure or a retention test, so this lesson was not exercised. Its safeguards remain necessary: incidental upward displacement while tipping cannot satisfy a grasp-and-hold task.

lessons_review.lesson: Before querying depth, identify the uncertainty and how each possible result would change the next action. Sample recognizable target or obstacle surfaces, rejecting hand, support, interior, and background returns that do not represent the intended feature. Estimate attitude from corresponding features distributed across the target or from a coherent surface, not from isolated similar-height samples. Reuse established geometry while observations remain consistent. When occlusion or pose tracking is the bottleneck, inspect the most informative available view and measured configuration, then revise the motion; obtain further depth only for the specific unresolved geometric decision.
lessons_review.why: Initial probes supplied useful target and support geometry. However, the policy collected 31 depth samples across three actions, and later sampling did not produce a reliable attitude check or resolve the unsafe orientation correction. Retain decision-driven probing, but emphasize feature correspondence, return classification, and changing the action when tracking rather than localization is the bottleneck.

lessons.lesson: Before approaching or changing contact, check the swept volume of the entire measured hand against both the target and its surroundings, including motion caused by rotation; support clearance alone is not target clearance. Arrange opposing contact regions around the intended grasp region rather than advancing a digit through the target. If an unsecured target shifts or tilts unexpectedly, treat this as possible contact: unload along an observed clear separating path without adding rotation, reobserve its support and attitude, then restore a task-compatible supported pose or select a revised approach.
lessons.why: The previews and reasoning emphasized the lowest hand point above the table. There were no hand-table contacts, yet open-hand target contact at step 2 produced tipping, and the subsequent rotation increased it substantially.

lessons.lesson: After near-contact motion, compare the achieved palm orientation and measured hand shape with the intended configuration before advancing. Unexpected orientation changes invalidate the previous digit-clearance estimate. Use brief, separate adjustments in verified clearance rather than correcting attitude in place beside an unsecured target. If tracking remains unreliable, choose another clearance-checked reachable configuration or approach instead of repeating corrections or retreats. Resume task motion once the achieved alignment and sweep are adequate, without chasing exact nominal attitude. Re-support an unreliably retained target before reconfiguring.
lessons.why: Step 2 reached the requested position closely but had a large orientation discrepancy. Step 3 responded with an in-place orientation correction while the hand remained beside the target, worsening the tip despite its shorter execution.

lessons.lesson: Before querying depth, identify the unresolved geometric decision and how the result will change the next action. Classify returns as target, hand, support, or background and use each only for its intended role. Estimate target attitude and motion from corresponding, spatially distributed features relative to stable surroundings, not similar heights of unrelated samples or palm attitude. If occlusion prevents correspondence, inspect the most informative available view and probe only the remaining ambiguity. Reuse established geometry while observations agree; when tracking is the bottleneck, revise the motion rather than collecting more localization samples.
lessons.why: Depth established useful geometry, but dense repeated sampling did not prevent the unsupported upright interpretation or the unsafe correction. The policy needed a coherent target-pose comparison and a response to measured tracking error, not another broad localization batch.

lessons.lesson: For a grasp or regrasp, once opposing-contact alignment and a clear closing sweep are established, close without unnecessary simultaneous reorientation and perform a cautious retention test. Verify that the target follows the hand without slipping and achieves the required displacement and attitude relative to stable surroundings. If retention is uncertain, re-support the target and revise contact placement before further transport. During a verified hold, preserve the intended pose rather than adopting measured drift, count only executed time with the required conditions maintained, and advance when those conditions are complete.
lessons.why: All executed actions kept the hand open. The observed height change occurred without a retained upright grasp, and the evaluator confirmed that neither the required lift nor hold was achieved. This preserves the untested but necessary completion safeguards.

reflections.diagnosis: The episode failed before establishing a grasp. Depth sensing successfully located the mug surfaces and tabletop, but the policy repeatedly used support clearance and separated fingertips as evidence that the whole hand would clear the mug. Large command-to-measurement orientation errors early in the episode made intended hand orientation an unreliable clearance model. Later open-hand approaches produced unilateral contact at step 7 and steps 10–14, while the policy continued describing the mug as upright without establishing its attitude from corresponding features. The maximum tilt reached 60.92 degrees. All 14 actions kept the gripper open, so there was no secured lift or retention test; the evaluator's 3.66 cm displacement did not constitute the requested upright lift and hold. Early repeated depth sampling and overhead adjustments added substantial cost without resolving the actual bottleneck: achieving a reachable, collision-free opposing-contact configuration and detecting unintended target motion.
reflections.failure_mode: Unsecured-target tipping during an open-hand approach, caused by incomplete target-clearance checks and inadequate motion/attitude monitoring, compounded by hand-orientation tracking errors. No grasp closure or verified hold occurred.

lessons_review.lesson: Before approaching or changing contact, check the swept volume of the entire measured hand against both the target and its surroundings, including motion caused by rotation; support clearance alone is not target clearance. Arrange opposing contact regions around the intended grasp region rather than advancing a digit through the target. If an unsecured target shifts or tilts unexpectedly, treat this as possible contact: unload along an observed clear separating path without adding rotation, reobserve its support and attitude, then restore a task-compatible supported pose or select a revised approach.
lessons_review.why: It partially helped: the hand avoided the table, unsafe low candidates were rejected at steps 12–13, and step 8 unloaded the earlier contact. However, the policy repeatedly checked fingertip separation and minimum height rather than enforcing whole-hand clearance from the mug. Contacts at steps 10–14 were followed by further approach instead of a revised contact corridor. Retain the principle but make the geometric checks and recovery choice more explicit.

lessons_review.lesson: After near-contact motion, compare the achieved palm orientation and measured hand shape with the intended configuration before advancing. Unexpected orientation changes invalidate the previous digit-clearance estimate. Use brief, separate adjustments in verified clearance rather than correcting attitude in place beside an unsecured target. If tracking remains unreliable, choose another clearance-checked reachable configuration or approach instead of repeating corrections or retreats. Resume task motion once the achieved alignment and sweep are adequate, without chasing exact nominal attitude. Re-support an unreliably retained target before reconfiguring.
lessons_review.why: Separate adjustments at steps 3–4 and 8–9 recovered more usable orientations after substantial tracking errors. The lesson was not inherently responsible for the detours, but its tracking check was incompletely applied: subsequent commands often inherited the latest measured orientation without preserving a stable grasp configuration. Step 14 also requested a poorly reachable pose. Strengthen the rule around observed tracking variation and choosing a stable reachable approach.

lessons_review.lesson: Before querying depth, identify the unresolved geometric decision and how the result will change the next action. Classify returns as target, hand, support, or background and use each only for its intended role. Estimate target attitude and motion from corresponding, spatially distributed features relative to stable surroundings, not similar heights of unrelated samples or palm attitude. If occlusion prevents correspondence, inspect the most informative available view and probe only the remaining ambiguity. Reuse established geometry while observations agree; when tracking is the bottleneck, revise the motion rather than collecting more localization samples.
lessons_review.why: Initial depth samples usefully distinguished the table and mug, but the reuse and correspondence requirements were largely not enforced. Broad sampling was repeated while the mug remained stationary early on. Later, additional surface points did not produce a reliable motion or tilt assessment, and the policy continued calling the mug upright through increasing contact-induced disturbance. Preserve this lesson with an explicit requirement to connect each query to the next manipulation decision.

lessons_review.lesson: For a grasp or regrasp, once opposing-contact alignment and a clear closing sweep are established, close without unnecessary simultaneous reorientation and perform a cautious retention test. Verify that the target follows the hand without slipping and achieves the required displacement and attitude relative to stable surroundings. If retention is uncertain, re-support the target and revise contact placement before further transport. During a verified hold, preserve the intended pose rather than adopting measured drift, count only executed time with the required conditions maintained, and advance when those conditions are complete.
lessons_review.why: No closing command was issued, so retention testing and hold verification were never exercised. There is no evidence that any recorded pose was ready for safe closure. Keep the conditional progression rule, emphasizing that verified contact placement should lead to closure rather than indefinite open-hand advancement.

lessons.lesson: Before changing contact, check the approach and closing paths of the contact pads and intervening hand links against the target's outer shape, including protrusions. Separated fingertips and clearance above the support do not establish target clearance. If a link may intersect the target before opposing contact regions surround the selected grasp region, reposition the open hand around the outer contour in clear space and verify the revised path. If an unsecured target moves or tilts during approach, unload along a clear separating direction, reassess its support, and choose a changed contact placement or restore a task-compatible supported pose before advancing.
lessons.why: The hand never contacted the table, yet it repeatedly contacted and disturbed the mug. Step 8 successfully unloaded the first contact, but later motions returned to an unsafe approach and eventually produced severe tipping. Whole-link target checks and a genuinely changed approach would address the failure more directly than additional support-height checks.

lessons.lesson: Use measured hand pose and joint shape, together with observed tracking variation, to judge the next motion's clearance; repeating an orientation command does not guarantee a translation-only sweep. After a brief near-contact motion, compare the achieved configuration and target response with the plan before continuing. If alignment changes enough to threaten clearance or the requested pose is poorly reached, make a separate adjustment in verified free space or choose another reachable approach. Resume when the achieved configuration is stable and task-compatible, preserving that intended alignment rather than repeatedly adopting drift or chasing exact nominal orientation. Re-support an unreliably held target before reconfiguring.
lessons.why: The first two actions had large orientation errors despite accurate palm positions. Separate adjustments later improved tracking, but orientation continued changing during approach, and the final requested pose was poorly reached. Clearance needed to account for actual hand configuration and control variability, not just the commanded quaternion.

lessons.lesson: Maintain a reusable estimate of target and support geometry from labeled observations. Before querying depth, identify the unresolved decision about clearance, contact placement, or target motion and how the result will change the next action. To assess motion or attitude, compare corresponding, spatially distributed target features relative to stable surroundings rather than heights of unrelated surface samples. If the relevant region is occluded, inspect the most informative available image or use a clearance-checked observation pose, then probe only the remaining ambiguity. Reuse geometry while observations agree; if tracking is the bottleneck, revise the motion instead of repeating localization.
lessons.why: The early geometry was established repeatedly while the mug remained stationary. Later sampling did not distinguish target motion and tilt reliably, especially as visibility worsened. Decision-directed probing would reduce redundant calls while concentrating sensing on the contact and attitude uncertainties that mattered.

lessons.lesson: For a grasp or regrasp, once measured opposing contact regions surround the selected target region and the closing sweep is clear, preserve the aligned palm pose and close rather than continuing to advance the open hand. Perform a cautious, task-compatible retention test and verify that the target follows without slipping or losing the required attitude relative to its surroundings. If retention is uncertain, re-support the target and revise contact placement. If retention is verified, complete the requested motion and hold while maintaining the intended pose, counting only executed time under the required conditions.
lessons.why: The episode ended after repeated open-hand approaches with no closure, secured lift, or hold. This supplies a concrete progression criterion after alignment is corrected; it does not recommend closing at an unsafe recorded pose or treating incidental displacement as successful retention.
